title: Hourglass Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: per-cell space-or-star checks versus measuring each row by its distance from the nearest edge and building it directly, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print an hourglass shape with 2n minus 1 rows, wide and solid at the top, narrowing down to a single star in the exact middle, then widening back out to a solid row at the bottom.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Sand Timer
blocks.text: Picture an actual hourglass sand timer, wide at the top chamber, pinched down to a single narrow neck in the middle where the sand passes through, and wide again at the bottom chamber. The pinch point is a single grain wide, exactly one star, with both sides mirroring each other around it.

blocks.text: With n = 1, the top and bottom chambers collapse into a single row, a single star.
No rows at all, so nothing is printed.
Since the diamond already established the distance-from-nearest-tip idea, it is worth checking exactly what has to change to turn a diamond inside out into an hourglass.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The same distance measurement, m equal to min of r and 2n minus r, still applies here, since this shape is still symmetric about its middle row, exactly like the diamond.

Observation 2: The genuine difference is which quantity grows and which one shrinks toward the middle, in the diamond the star region grew toward the middle while the gap shrank, here it is the exact opposite, the star region shrinks toward the middle while the gap grows.

Observation 3: Testing this against a small example, n equal to 4, confirms it: the middle row, m equal to n, has the largest gap and the smallest star count, exactly one star, the pinch point of the hourglass.

Observation 4: Once that swap is made, gap equals m minus 1 instead of n minus m, and stars equal 2 times n minus m, plus 1, instead of 2m minus 1, the same direct-construction and distance-measurement techniques from the diamond still apply without any further changes.
That single swap, growing and shrinking trading places, is the entire difference between deriving this formula from scratch and deriving it directly from the diamond already solved.

For every row, first work out its distance from the nearer edge, top or bottom, then use two nested loops, printing a single space or star one character at a time based on the leading gap for that row.

items: Loop over every row r, from 1 to 2n minus 1.
Compute m, the distance of this row from whichever edge is closer, top or bottom.
Compute the gap, m minus 1, and the star count, 2 times n minus m, plus 1.
Check every column, printing a space while still in the gap, and a star afterward.
After finishing a row, move to the next line.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: find the distance from the nearest edge, then print space or star per column

codes.python:
def hourglass_pattern(n):
    total_rows = 2 * n - 1
    for r in range(1, total_rows + 1):          # r counts every row, top edge to bottom edge
        m = min(r, 2 * n - r)                     # this row's distance from the nearest tip
        gap = m - 1
        stars = 2 * (n - m) + 1
        for j in range(gap + stars):               # check every column this row actually uses
            if j < gap:
                print(" ", end="")                    # still inside the leading gap
            else:
                print("*", end="")                    # inside the star region
        print()                                    # move to the next line after the row


if __name__ == "__main__":
    hourglass_pattern(4)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: m is computed once per row exactly as with the diamond, but here it drives a gap that grows toward the middle instead of shrinking.
gap and stars are derived from m using formulas with the growth direction swapped from the diamond, m minus 1 and 2 times n minus m, plus 1, instead of n minus m and 2m minus 1.
The inner loop still checks each column one at a time, printing a single character per iteration, which is exactly the inefficiency the optimized version removes.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every row correctly measures its distance from the nearer edge, and every column within that row is checked individually against the resulting gap.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since the total stars across the full hourglass is proportional to n squared, and every position is checked one at a time.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: once the gap and star count for a row are known, checking every column individually adds nothing, both regions can be built directly in a single operation each, exactly as with the plain centered pyramid solved earlier.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column works but is wasteful: once m, and therefore the gap and star count, are already known for a row, printing them one character at a time repeats a decision a single direct construction could make in one step.

What stays the same as the diamond: the distance measurement, m equal to min of r and 2n minus r, and the overall direct-construction technique both transfer unchanged.

What is different here: the roles of the gap and the star region are swapped, the gap now grows toward the middle, m minus 1, and the star count now shrinks toward the middle, 2 times n minus m, plus 1.

Can the same direct-construction technique be reused unchanged: yes, a repeat operation still builds the gap in one step and another builds the star region, regardless of which one is growing and which is shrinking.

The core idea: compute m once per row, then build the gap and the star region directly using the swapped formulas, exactly as with the diamond.

For each row, compute its distance from the nearer edge once, then build the leading gap and the star region directly, using one operation each, and concatenate them into a single row string. This removes all per cell branching, needing only one print call per row.
For each row, compute its distance from the nearer edge once, then build the gap and the shrinking star region directly and print the whole row with a single call.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: find the distance from the nearest edge, build the row directly

codes.python:
def hourglass_pattern(n):
    total_rows = 2 * n - 1
    for r in range(1, total_rows + 1):          # r counts every row, top edge to bottom edge
        m = min(r, 2 * n - r)                     # this row's distance from the nearest tip
        row = " " * (m - 1) + "*" * (2 * (n - m) + 1)  # build the gap and star run directly
        print(row)                               # one print call per row instead of per character


if __name__ == "__main__":
    hourglass_pattern(4)

blocks.text: This works because m, exactly as with the diamond, correctly measures every row's distance from the nearer edge, and because the gap and star formulas here are simply the diamond's formulas with growth and shrinkage swapped, m minus 1 instead of n minus m, and 2 times n minus m, plus 1, instead of 2m minus 1; a direct repeat operation still constructs each region in one step, producing the correct pinch at the middle row where m equals n.

A direct repeat operation builds the m minus 1 space gap, and another builds the 2 times n minus m, plus 1, star region, the same construction technique as the diamond, just fed the swapped formulas.
Concatenating those two pieces and printing once per row completes the entire hourglass, correctly narrowing to a single star exactly when m equals n.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, but with no per cell branching and only O(n) print calls instead of O(n squared) checks.
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly in one operation, so instead of printing each one separately, all rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

items: Every row is still built directly from its own m value, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is collecting each finished row instead of printing it immediately.
Joining all 2n minus 1 rows with newline characters assembles the complete hourglass as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole shape, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: An hourglass is the diamond seen earlier turned inside out, instead of a growing gap moving toward the middle, the star count itself shrinks toward the middle while the gap grows, pinching down to a single star before widening back out symmetrically.

items: Reusing the diamond formula directly without swapping which quantity grows and which one shrinks toward the middle row.
Miscounting the pinch point, the middle row should always be exactly one star, never zero and never more than one.
Forgetting the n = 0 edge case, where nothing at all should be printed.

blocks.text: Recognizing that an hourglass is a diamond with the growth direction flipped, gap growing instead of shrinking toward the middle, is a fast way to derive its formula directly from one already solved, rather than working it out from scratch.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how is this related to the diamond", think: it is the same distance measurement, m equal to min of r and 2n minus r, with growth and shrinkage swapped between the gap and the star region.
If the interviewer says "where is the narrowest point", think: exactly at the middle row, where m equals n, producing a gap of n minus 1 and exactly 1 star.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build every row first, join with newlines, print once.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: per cell checks in the brute force version, one formula built row per print call in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: pattern printing that reuses the diamond's distance-from-nearest-edge measurement, but with the growth direction inverted, the star region shrinks toward the middle while the gap grows, instead of the other way around.

Core Idea: compute m, a row's distance from the nearer edge, exactly as with the diamond, then build a gap of m minus 1 spaces and a star region of 2n minus 2m plus 1 stars, the diamond's formulas with growth and shrinkage swapped.
Time: O(n squared) checks for the brute force, O(n) output calls for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: a new shape can sometimes be derived entirely by swapping which quantity grows and which one shrinks in a formula already solved.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape with enough care; deriving it directly from the diamond by naming the swap explicitly is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: same m as the diamond, but gap equals m minus 1 and stars equal 2n minus 2m plus 1, growth and shrinkage swapped.
